title: strings and character sequences
concepts: A string algorithm operates on an ordered sequence and must define what one element means
C# strings are immutable UTF-16 sequences; indexing and Length count UTF-16 code units rather than user-perceived characters
Unicode scalar values and grapheme clusters differ from UTF-16 code units
Character equality may be ordinal, culture-sensitive, case-sensitive, or normalized according to the problem definition
Prefix, suffix, substring, and frequency relationships support common string problem reductions
Linear scans, two-ended scans, frequency counts, and prefix-function matching solve different string tasks
Hash-based string matching has collision risk and requires a correctness-aware design

practiceProblems.name: Valid Palindrome
practiceProblems.statement: Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome after converting uppercase letters to lowercase and removing every non-alphanumeric character; otherwise return false.
constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

practiceProblems.name: Valid Anagram
practiceProblems.statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses every character the same number of times; order may differ.
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters.

practiceProblems.name: Reverse String
practiceProblems.statement: Reverse the input character array s in place using O(1) extra memory.
constraints: s[i] is a printable ASCII character.

practiceProblems.name: First Unique Character in a String
